A Very Brief History of Ypsilanti Native Americans Long before Ypsilanti was known as Ypsilanti, the area was inhabited primarily by the Potawatomi and Wyandot Indians, among other Native American tribes. ○ Open citation. They built trails throughout the city, one of which is now Michigan Avenue (highlighted in yellow), and settlements just south of present-day Michigan Avenue Jump to Edgenote (triangle also highlighted in yellow). Photo credit : Mark Maynard 1931 Hinsdale map of current-day Ypsilanti area showing Native American settlements prior to 1800s Return to narrative By the 1830s, Native Americans were forcibly removed from newly incorporated City of Ypsilanti Jump to Edgenote and the larger Southeast Michigan area as White Europeans developed trading posts and villages in the area. Throughout this time and the decades that followed, Ypsilanti became critical settlement for Black slaves escaping the south along the Underground Railroad Jump to Edgenote . Where these Black communities were allowed to settle isn’t surprising. Learn more about how Ypsilanti got it's unique name cityofypsilanti.com › Return to narrative Learn more about the Underground Railroad in Ypsilanti youtube.com › Return to narrative Black Americans The vast majority of Black residents were segregated to the southside of Ypslanti Jump to Edgenote – south of Michigan Avenue – where the former Native American settlements were located. Throughout the late 1800s and early 1900s, life for Black residents of Ypsilanti told a similar story to other Black Americans at the time – a story of segregation. Segregated homes. Segregated schools. Segregated restaurants. A former Black Ypsilanti teacher, Marguerite Eaglin, tells a story Jump to Edgenote of how segregation looked like during the 1950s in the city. African American Ypsilanti, 1910. - Google My Maps google.com › Return to narrative “ They finally served us, but they burned the bread ” — Marguerite Eaglin, ca. 1980s Return to narrative “ … and the fact that because I was black, there were restaurants downtown that didn’t want us to come and eat. My children told me the story about how good Haab’s french fries were, but they had to stand outside and buy them from the window if they wanted any. I wasn’t aware of that. My friend Yvonne Williams and I would go downtown for lunch and we’d go into a place and sit and sit and sit. I was teaching school, so I only had so much time for lunch. Nobody actively insulted us, but they just didn’t wait on us. They just ignored us like we weren’t there. Finally in one place, I said, “Look, I have to go back to school. Do you know when we could get served, please?” They finally served us, but they burned the bread.” – Marguerite Eaglin, ca. 1980s Jump to Edgenote  …[truncated]
